pages.title: Concurrency specification
pages.markdown:
Draft 0.2 extension. The language MUST support concurrent application code with ownership, effect and cancellation rules that remain meaningful across native and WebAssembly backends. The proposed default is structured concurrency; shared-memory and distributed protocols add explicit guarantees rather than inheriting them from task syntax.

# 1 Three distinct properties

Concurrency permits overlapping lifetimes and interleaved progress. Parallelism executes work simultaneously on multiple processing resources. Distribution introduces independent failure and communication boundaries. An `Async` effect does not imply parallelism, fairness, or distributed delivery guarantees.

The initial execution abstractions are local tasks, transferable tasks, bounded channels, scoped parallel work, and supervised long-lived services. The source semantics must specify permitted observations independently of a particular event-loop implementation. Determinism requires additional conditions; ordinary concurrency can observe different valid schedules.

# 2 Structured tasks

A task belongs to a scope whose lifetime bounds its captures. A scope cannot successfully release borrowed state while a child still uses it. Leaving the scope either observes completion or follows a declared cancellation-and-join protocol. Dropping a task handle MUST NOT silently detach execution.

```haskell
loadPair :: forall r. using (io :: Io r) =>
            Request -> Request
            ->{Async r, IO r, Cancel r, Diverge}
              Result LoadError (Bytes, Bytes)
loadPair left right = withScope $ \s -> do
  a <- spawn s (\() -> fetch left)
  b <- spawn s (\() -> fetch right)
  joinAllOrCancel s a b
```

This is a proposed library API. The combinator observes both tasks, selects the documented failure policy, requests sibling cancellation when needed, and waits for cleanup acknowledgment before returning. Its `LoadError` or task outcome contract includes cancellation and supported task failures. It cannot promise bounded completion if a child or foreign dependency can remain stuck.

Long-lived background services attach to an explicit supervisor or root scope. Supervision controls restart and reporting; it does not imply state rollback or exactly-once external effects.

# 3 Ownership across tasks

| Operation | Required ownership condition |
| --- | --- |
| Spawn local work | Captures remain valid for the scope; no incompatible aliasing during interleaving |
| Spawn migratable work | Captures and results satisfy a `Send`-like transfer interface |
| Share references across threads | The referent satisfies a `Sync`-like interface and the borrow remains live |
| Send an owned message | Ownership transfers at the channel's specified commit point |
| Share mutable state | Use an approved synchronization abstraction with an invariant |

The marker names are proposed and their implementations must be checked or explicitly trusted. An immutable wrapper around a thread-affine foreign pointer is not automatically transferable. A local task can still create a logical race by interleaving operations; staying on one thread does not make every state protocol atomic.

The type system must model borrows held across suspension. The initial default SHOULD reject ordinary blocking mutex guards across calls whose effects include `Async`, with separate async-aware abstractions where appropriate. This prevents a common problem but does not prove arbitrary deadlock freedom.

# 4 Cancellation and resource completion

Cancellation is a cooperative request delivered at defined suspension or polling points. It is a distinct control effect or outcome, not an arbitrary exception injected between any two machine instructions. Short, explicitly scoped masking regions may protect ownership transitions; unbounded masking must not hide a progress obligation.

The API distinguishes cancellation requested, cancellation observed, cleanup completed, and operation outcome. A foreign call or host operation may continue after a request. Owned buffers and callback registrations remain live until the operation's protocol permits release.

A channel send race must say whether ownership transferred. Failure before commit returns the message; after commit, the receiver or channel owns it. An API that loses a linear message when cancellation races with send is invalid. `select` and `race` combinators must dispose of losing registrations and tasks according to their protocols; dropping a future is not a universal undo operation.

Shutdown has a declared policy for unfinished cleanup and unresponsive children. Forced process or component termination is an outer containment action with explicit resource and external-outcome consequences. Structured concurrency guarantees lifetime discipline, not that every cleanup action eventually succeeds.

# 5 Channels and actors

Bounded channels are the default proposal so backpressure and queue capacity are explicit. Their contracts specify ownership transfer, closure, blocked send and receive behavior, cancellation, and the ordering actually guaranteed. Global total order and delivery exactly once are not inferred from a channel type.

Actors are a library abstraction owning private state and receiving typed messages. Message protocols can be represented using typestate or session-style interfaces. Such interfaces can establish legal local communication sequences; global progress requires additional constraints on participants, topology, scheduling and failure.

Actor restart and hot replacement preserve mailbox contents, reply obligations, resource handles and unknown external outcomes when required. Replacing the handler does not by itself validate those transitions.

# 6 Shared memory and atomics

The language memory model must define permitted concurrent observations and synchronize-with relationships. Safe code prevents data races; it does not automatically make a multi-step operation linearizable. Synchronization libraries package invariants, ownership transfer rules, and proofs at their logical linearization points.

Atomic operations expose the supported ordering choices explicitly. Release/acquire proofs must establish an actual synchronizes-with relation for the relevant communication; merely labeling two operations does not create one. Relaxed operations provide only their specified guarantees, and the compiler cannot infer ordinary inter-thread happens-before facts from them.

Low-level atomic libraries need memory-reclamation protocols as well as atomic instructions. ABA, premature reclamation, and callback lifetime can invalidate a lock-free structure even when all individual accesses use atomics. Epochs, hazard pointers or another chosen reclamation scheme require their own contracts.

Backends MUST preserve the source memory model through native or Wasm lowering. Unsupported orderings or atomics cannot silently become unsynchronized accesses. Initial high-level APIs should use proved locks and channels; lock-free algorithms are an advanced library boundary.

# 7 Software transactional memory

A Haskell-like STM library is a proposed addition. `atomically` evaluates a transaction over versioned shared cells and commits atomically or retries. Transactional code is restricted to approved STM effects and total logical computation; it cannot perform arbitrary I/O, FFI, suspension, or irreversible resource consumption inside a retryable body.

`retry` suspends until relevant state changes under the selected runtime contract. `orElse` composes alternatives with documented retry behavior. Transactions may be re-executed, so captured ownership and allocations must obey a rollback-safe discipline. Starvation freedom and fairness are additional claims, not consequences of atomic commit.

External effects occur after commit through an explicit protocol, such as a durable outbox when the application needs crash recovery. An in-memory transaction plus a network request is not a distributed atomic transaction.

# 8 Proofs and testing

The design supports library-specific proofs of state invariants, linearizability, protocol adherence, resource accounting, and temporal progress. Each proof identifies environmental and scheduling assumptions. A race-free program can still deadlock, starve, leak logical work, or produce wrong results.

Testing infrastructure SHOULD include deterministic scheduler control, cancellation injection at supported points, and replayable execution traces. Bounded schedule exploration and model checking are useful counterexample tools. Their bounds remain explicit; successful testing is not a universal proof.

Lock ordering can prove freedom from selected lock cycles. Session types can prove selected protocol properties. Neither mechanism alone proves that an arbitrary service always responds, particularly across foreign calls and network failures.

# 9 Backends and scheduler capabilities

The same structured-task API can have a cooperative single-threaded implementation or a multithreaded implementation where its contract permits. Code explicitly requiring parallel execution must request that capability or accept an explicit fallback policy. The library must not conceal unsupported parallelism behind a performance promise.

Blocking calls use an offload or host suspension contract supported by the target. A browser host without such support cannot satisfy an arbitrary blocking-native-call abstraction by running it on its event loop. Scheduler work budgets and cooperative yield points are part of responsiveness policies, not proof that all tasks terminate.

WASI async integration preserves completion, stream backpressure and cancellation rules. Native async and component async may use different runtime mechanisms while implementing the same source-level contract.

# 10 Concurrent hot replacement

A module update is itself a concurrent protocol. Its activation point defines which version accepts new calls, which handles and queues remain shared, and how outstanding operations are attributed. State snapshots need synchronization or a revalidation guard before migration commits.

Draining tasks includes children, foreign operations and callbacks, not just exported function frames. Version coexistence requires a cross-version state protocol. A shared state invariant cannot be changed while old code continues assuming the previous invariant without a relation that supports both.

Liveness proofs cover the updater and scheduler together. Repeated updates must not indefinitely restart work or lose progress. The runtime's cancellation, fairness and migration policies are therefore dependencies of temporal contracts.

# 11 Initial scope

Implement structured scopes, cooperative cancellation, bounded channels, local tasks and explicit blocking-call handling first. Add transfer-checked parallel tasks and proved synchronization primitives next. STM, session-style protocol libraries and lock-free structures can build on that foundation; their interfaces and evidence should remain replaceable modules where the runtime supports it.

Required rejection cases include borrowed state escaping its scope, unsafely sharing a thread-affine handle, losing a message during cancelled send, performing FFI inside a retryable transaction, and claiming a timeout stopped a foreign operation without acknowledgment.

The draft 0.2 surface uses layout, equations and unqualified `do`. See [Surface syntax and grammar](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_18d4c95146a48191a722223f1e8dd18a) and [Runtime capabilities, effects and sequencing](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_f7f7e6466b348191803f2f900098b667) for formal syntax, runtime arguments, effect-polymorphic calls and sequencing-module selection.

| Send an owned message | Ownership transfers at the channel's specified commit point |
| Share mutable state | Use an approved synchronization abstraction with an invariant |

The marker names are proposed and their implementations must be checked or explicitly trusted. An immutable wrapper around a thread-affine foreign pointer is not automatically transferable. A local task can still create a logical race by interleaving operations; staying on one thread does not make every state protocol atomic.

The type system must model borrows held across suspension. The initial default SHOULD reject ordinary blocking mutex guards across calls whose effects include `Async`, with separate async-aware abstractions where appropriate. This prevents a common problem but does not prove arbitrary deadlock freedom.
# 4 Cancellation and resource completion

Cancellation is a cooperative request delivered at defined suspension or polling points. It is a distinct control effect or outcome, not an arbitrary exception injected between any two machine instructions. Short, explicitly scoped masking regions may protect ownership transitions; unbounded masking must not hide a progress obligation.

The API distinguishes cancellation requested, cancellation observed, cleanup completed, and operation outcome. A foreign call or host operation may continue after a request. Owned buffers and callback registrations remain live until the operation's protocol permits release.

A channel send race must say whether ownership transferred. Failure before commit returns the message; after commit, the receiver or channel owns it. An API that loses a linear message when cancellation races with send is invalid. `select` and `race` combinators must dispose of losing registrations and tasks according to their protocols; dropping a future is not a universal undo operation.

Shutdown has a declared policy for unfinished cleanup and unresponsive children. Forced process or component termination is an outer containment action with explicit resource and external-outcome consequences. Structured concurrency guarantees lifetime discipline, not that every cleanup action eventually succeeds.
# 5 Channels and actors

Bounded channels are the default proposal so backpressure and queue capacity are explicit. Their contracts specify ownership transfer, closure, blocked send and receive behavior, cancellation, and the ordering actually guaranteed. Global total order and delivery exactly once are not inferred from a channel type.

Actors are a library abstraction owning private state and receiving typed messages. Message protocols can be represented using typestate or session-style interfaces. Such interfaces can establish legal local communication sequences; global progress requires additional constraints on participants, topology, scheduling and failure.

Actor restart and hot replacement preserve mailbox contents, reply obligations, resource handles and unknown external outcomes when required. Replacing the handler does not by itself validate those transitions.
# 6 Shared memory and atomics

The language memory model must define permitted concurrent observations and synchronize-with relationships. Safe code prevents data races; it does not automatically make a multi-step operation linearizable. Synchronization libraries package invariants, ownership transfer rules, and proofs at their logical linearization points.

Atomic operations expose the supported ordering choices explicitly. Release/acquire proofs must establish an actual synchronizes-with relation for the relevant communication; merely labeling two operations does not create one. Relaxed operations provide only their specified guarantees, and the compiler cannot infer ordinary inter-thread happens-before facts from them.

Low-level atomic libraries need memory-reclamation protocols as well as atomic instructions. ABA, premature reclamation, and callback lifetime can invalidate a lock-free structure even when all individual accesses use atomics. Epochs, hazard pointers or another chosen reclamation scheme require their own contracts.

Backends MUST preserve the source memory model through native or Wasm lowering. Unsupported orderings or atomics cannot silently become unsynchronized accesses. Initial high-level APIs should use proved locks and channels; lock-free algorithms are an advanced library boundary.
# 7 Software transactional memory

A Haskell-like STM library is a proposed addition. `atomically` evaluates a transaction over versioned shared cells and commits atomically or retries. Transactional code is restricted to approved STM effects and total logical computation; it cannot perform arbitrary I/O, FFI, suspension, or irreversible resource consumption inside a retryable body.

`retry` suspends until relevant state changes under the selected runtime contract. `orElse` composes alternatives with documented retry behavior. Transactions may be re-executed, so captured ownership and allocations must obey a rollback-safe discipline. Starvation freedom and fairness are additional claims, not consequences of atomic commit.

External effects occur after commit through an explicit protocol, such as a durable outbox when the application needs crash recovery. An in-memory transaction plus a network request is not a distributed atomic transaction.
# 8 Proofs and testing

The design supports library-specific proofs of state invariants, linearizability, protocol adherence, resource accounting, and temporal progress. Each proof identifies environmental and scheduling assumptions. A race-free program can still deadlock, starve, leak logical work, or produce wrong results.

Testing infrastructure SHOULD include deterministic scheduler control, cancellation injection at supported points, and replayable execution traces. Bounded schedule exploration and model checking are useful counterexample tools. Their bounds remain explicit; successful testing is not a universal proof.

Lock ordering can prove freedom from selected lock cycles. Session types can prove selected protocol properties. Neither mechanism alone proves that an arbitrary service always responds, particularly across foreign calls and network failures.
# 9 Backends and scheduler capabilities

The same structured-task API can have a cooperative single-threaded implementation or a multithreaded implementation where its contract permits. Code explicitly requiring parallel execution must request that capability or accept an explicit fallback policy. The library must not conceal unsupported parallelism behind a performance promise.

Blocking calls use an offload or host suspension contract supported by the target. A browser host without such support cannot satisfy an arbitrary blocking-native-call abstraction by running it on its event loop. Scheduler work budgets and cooperative yield points are part of responsiveness policies, not proof that all tasks terminate.

WASI async integration preserves completion, stream backpressure and cancellation rules. Native async and component async may use different runtime mechanisms while implementing the same source-level contract.
# 10 Concurrent hot replacement

A module update is itself a concurrent protocol. Its activation point defines which version accepts new calls, which handles and queues remain shared, and how outstanding operations are attributed. State snapshots need synchronization or a revalidation guard before migration commits.

Draining tasks includes children, foreign operations and callbacks, not just exported function frames. Version coexistence requires a cross-version state protocol. A shared state invariant cannot be changed while old code continues assuming the previous invariant without a relation that supports both.

Liveness proofs cover the updater and scheduler together. Repeated updates must not indefinitely restart work or lose progress. The runtime's cancellation, fairness and migration policies are therefore dependencies of temporal contracts.
# 11 Initial scope

Implement structured scopes, cooperative cancellation, bounded channels, local tasks and explicit blocking-call handling first. Add transfer-checked parallel tasks and proved synchronization primitives next. STM, session-style protocol libraries and lock-free structures can build on that foundation; their interfaces and evidence should remain replaceable modules where the runtime supports it.

Required rejection cases include borrowed state escaping its scope, unsafely sharing a thread-affine handle, losing a message during cancelled send, performing FFI inside a retryable transaction, and claiming a timeout stopped a foreign operation without acknowledgment.

The draft 0.2 surface uses layout, equations and unqualified `do`. # Core notation

```haskell
module Example where
  twice :: Nat -> Nat
  twice x = x + x

  data Vec (n :: Nat) (a :: Type) where
    Nil  :: Vec 0 a
    Cons :: forall n. a -> Vec n a -> Vec (n + 1) a

  first :: forall a n region.
           Ref region (Vec (n + 1) a) -> Ref region a
  first xs = case xs of
    Cons x rest -> x
```

`f x y` is curried application, `::` introduces a signature, and `case ... of` performs pattern matching. Pattern matching a borrowed value uses checked borrow-pattern elaboration; it does not move fields out of the referent. `Ref` and `Mut` are library-visible reference types with region indices. Functions consume or borrow according to their types; using a Haskell-like surface does not grant implicit duplication of resources.

Kinds, types and values share term syntax. `Type`, `Prop`, `Nat`, equality and type constructors are checked by elaboration rather than by a second restricted type-expression grammar. `Vec (n + 1) a` uses a computed index. `(n :: Nat) -> Vec n a` is a dependent function type; `Sigma (n :: Nat). Vec n a` is a dependent pair. `forall` binds implicit parameters; explicit annotations remain necessary where inference cannot determine them. Unbound signature variables are errors in this draft, rather than silently generalized.
# Strictness and effects

Arguments evaluate left to right, after the function expression. Application associates left, arrows associate right. Partial application creates a closure; the type of each arrow states the effects at that application step. `a -> b ->{IO r} c` is pure when given only the first argument and effectful when given the second.

`a -> b` means a pure total arrow. `a ->{|e} b` has an open effect row. `a ->{Async r, Net r | e} b` has named effects and a row tail. A local definition without a signature may infer effects; an explicit pure signature cannot hide them. `Diverge` remains explicit whenever termination is not established.

There is no `async` declaration modifier or special `await` expression. A suspendable call returns its ordinary result under an `Async` effect. Task handles remain explicit values when work is spawned. Because evaluation is strict, `spawn s (fetch request)` starts evaluating `fetch` too early; write `spawn s (\() -> fetch request)`.
# Layout and lexing

The EBNF consumes explicit `{`, `;` and `}` tokens after a deterministic layout pass. `where`, `of`, `do` and `let` introduce a layout block unless followed by an explicit `{`. The next non-comment token starts the block at its column. At a later logical line start, equal indentation inserts `;`, lower indentation closes nested implicit blocks, and greater indentation continues the current item. The first item receives no inserted separator.

An implicit block must indent farther than its enclosing implicit block. An explicit delimiter shields enclosing layout while it is open; layout blocks begun inside it still use their own indentation. Closing `)`, `]` or an explicit `}` first closes implicit blocks opened inside that delimiter. End of file closes remaining implicit blocks. `in` closes the nearest applicable implicit `let` block and any nested implicit blocks; it must not cross an unmatched explicit delimiter. A `let` statement in `do` has no `in` and closes by indentation. Use explicit braces for empty blocks or a form the layout rule cannot express. There is no parser-error-based insertion rule.

Comments are `--` to end of line and nestable `{- ... -}` blocks. Tabs are rejected in indentation. Line endings normalize to LF. Identifiers are ASCII in this draft; string and character contents are Unicode scalar values. Strings support `\\`, `\"`, `\'`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, and `\u{HEX}` with a valid scalar. Comment recognition has priority over symbol identifiers. Reserved punctuation is matched longest first, including `::`, `->`, `<-`, `=>`, `[|`, `|]`, `$(` and multiplicities. Dot is qualification or projection, never decimal punctuation except inside a numeric token. `f(x)` parses as applying `f` to `x`; `f(x,y)` supplies one tuple argument, not two curried arguments.

All quoted alphabetic terminals in the EBNF are reserved. `async`, `await`, `pure`, `spawn`, `join`, `delay`, `force`, `borrow` and `mutBorrow` are ordinary library names, not control syntax. Bare `_` is a pattern wildcard or elaboration hole; a hole cannot survive a deployable build.
# Operators and binding

The parser records an infix chain, then a fixity pass resolves it using the imported, unambiguous operator declarations. Fixity precedences range from 0 to 9; equal-precedence operators must have compatible associativity or require parentheses. There is no default for an undeclared operator. Application and projection bind tighter than infix operators; `$` is reserved right-associative application below all ordinary infix operators. Type annotations and arrows bind more loosely than expression operators. Prefix negation binds to one postfixed atomic term; write `-(f x)` to negate an application result.

The prelude declares arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and composition fixities. Comparisons are nonassociative. Local fixity declarations do not change the interpretation of already imported code. Parenthesized named binders before an arrow are dependent binders; a caller cannot reinterpret `(x :: A) -> B` as a value annotation followed by an arrow.

`%0`, `%1`, `%aff` and `%many` annotate erased, linear, affine and unrestricted arrow usage. These are constraints checked with the resource calculus, not a completed soundness result. Runtime capability parameters use `using (io :: Io r) => ...`. `with (io = selectedIO) in expression` supplies a lexical binding. `f @{io = selectedIO}` supplies an explicit dictionary at a call. No thread-local runtime lookup is implied.
# Declarations and abstractions

`signature` declares an abstraction with abstract types, operations and laws. `module M (S :: Signature) where ...` accepts a module parameter. `instance` implements a signature; `implicit instance` makes it eligible for unique dictionary resolution. Abstract module identity and associated types preserve the OCaml/Backpack-style abstraction boundary. These forms share one elaboration model, rather than creating unrelated module and trait systems.

`proof`, `spec`, `stage` and `corec` decorate signatures and matching equations. `rewrite` and `target rewrite` carry typed metavariable binders, a match, replacement, optional requirements and justification. Such a rule changes optimized program code only after proof checking; it does not extend definitional equality. `foreign import` declares ABI operations with explicit effects. `upgrade` names migration fields checked by the upgrade schema. WIT itself retains its own standard grammar.

Typed quotation is `[| expression |]`, with `$(code)` for a splice. `quoteDecls where ...` quotes declarations. `generate do ...` executes a checked generator. A macro invocation uses a balanced token tree; its expansion is hygienic and must parse and elaborate under this same language. Cross-module expansion does not bypass stage dependency checks.
# Sequencing

All sequencing uses unqualified `do`. Its interpretation is chosen by an in-scope sequencing module, with direct effect sequencing as the defined default. A custom interpretation must be explicit in the enclosing module or signature; the compiler does not infer short-circuiting merely because a result type happens to be `Result`.

`x <- action` binds according to that module, `let x = value` introduces a pure local binding, and the final expression supplies the block's result. Refutable patterns require an explicit case or an interpretation with a declared typed failure operation. A discarded linear result requires a valid consumption operation. The companion runtime and sequencing specification defines the distinction between control effects, result composition and runtime capabilities.
# Validation boundary

The EBNF defines a proposed concrete syntax, with the lexical and layout rules in this chapter. It is not a type checker, parser implementation or mechanized metatheory. Context checks still enforce legal declarations in signatures, complete module implementations, coverage, totality, effect rows, resource usage, module coherence, proof obligations and stage ordering. The grammar deliberately permits some forms that these later checks must reject.

Draft 0.2 design decision: ordinary function definitions, effect-polymorphic suspension, lexical runtime evidence, and unqualified typeclass/module-driven `do`. The grammar and examples use a strict Haskell-like surface.

# Three independent choices

| Choice | Representation | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What a computation may do | Effect row | Suspension, I/O, cancellation, divergence and other observations |
| Which implementation executes it | Lexical capability/module arguments and handlers | Scheduler, I/O driver, allocation and host integration |
| How intermediate results compose | Sequencing module selected for `do` | Direct binding, typed short-circuiting or an explicitly modeled computation abstraction |

These choices can be composed. Changing a scheduler does not automatically change how `Result` binds; changing a `do` instance does not grant access to the filesystem or erase suspension effects.

# Ordinary functions with suspension effects

```haskell
loadPair :: forall r. using (io :: Io r) =>
            Request -> Request
            ->{Async r, IO r, Cancel r, Diverge}
              Result LoadError (Bytes, Bytes)
loadPair left right = withScope $ \s -> do
  a <- spawn s (\() -> fetch left)
  b <- spawn s (\() -> fetch right)
  joinAllOrCancel s a b
```

`fetch`, `spawn` and `joinAllOrCancel` are ordinary operations with declared effects. This block uses direct sequencing: `a` and `b` are handles and the final value is a `Result`. There is no future wrapper automatically inserted into every function result. The explicit task handle represents independently scheduled work.

The API contract specifies that spawn either produces a valid scoped handle or follows its typed task-failure/cancellation protocol, and that scope exit joins cleanup. `Diverge` records the possibility that an external dependency or cleanup never completes. The notation does not establish fairness or bounded latency.

A call's effects flow into its caller unless an appropriate handler discharges them. A pure callback cannot call a suspending operation. Higher-order APIs should quantify over effect rows rather than duplicate sync and async variants. This removes a special syntactic and return-type category, while retaining a static distinction between computations that can and cannot suspend.

# Runtime parameters and implicit passing

The `io` parameter is real runtime evidence, not an erased proof. It is passed explicitly in the core. Surface `using` permits lexical implicit passing, and `f @{io = chosen}` makes the argument explicit at a call. Implementations may specialize a statically known dictionary or use checked dispatch; neither optimization is a guaranteed zero-cost theorem.

Runtime identity `r` ties operations, registrations, task handles and dependent proof assumptions to their runtime. It is not freely coercible across runtimes. Runtime creation introduces a fresh identity; its scope prevents dependent handles and borrows from escaping unless an owned runtime package supports that escape.

No global or thread-local default runtime is searched. The nearest explicitly introduced lexical provider binds a capability name; multiple candidates at the same resolution level are an error. Closures capture the provider and its lifetime when created. Calling the closure in a different runtime scope does not rebind its dependencies.

Use small capabilities where possible: scheduling, network access, filesystem handles, time and allocation need not be bundled in one authority. `Io r` in examples is a convenient selected interface, not mandatory access to every OS service. Compile-time capabilities are separate from runtime ones.

# Handlers and entry points

`with (io = runtime.io) in body` supplies evidence; it does not by itself remove effects. A runtime entry function installs the handler and exposes its residual effects. The model is schematically:

```text
body : A with effects {Async r, IO r, Cancel r | e}
handler : handles those effects using Runtime r
run handler body : Outcome A with effects residual(handler, e)
```

This is a typing judgment, not source syntax. Residual effects can include host I/O, failure, allocation and divergence. An event loop may suspend host execution; it cannot claim to synchronously return a result merely because it handles `Async`. The browser entry adapter exposes a Promise/callback boundary as appropriate, while internal calls retain direct-style source syntax.

A handler receives a one-shot continuation with its captured resources and region constraints. It may resume it once, transfer it into an owned suspended task, or cancel it through a cleanup protocol. It may not silently discard linear obligations or clone mutable borrows. General multishot handlers require separate duplicability evidence and are outside the initial safe async handler subset.

# Unqualified do through modules and typeclasses

The language has one `do` spelling. A sequencing interpretation is a module implementing a checked compiler-known signature. The module contains its result/computation families, binding operations, permitted effects, continuation-usage rules and laws. Implicit dictionary syntax is convenience for passing this module; explicit module parameters support Backpack-like wiring and abstract associated types.

The initial direct interpretation executes each statement, binds its ordinary value and continues. The initial `Result` interpretation executes a statement, inspects its `Result`, continues with the success payload or returns the failure. `Option` can use the same one-shot structure. No interpretation is selected solely from the appearance of a `Result` in an ordinary function's return type: direct code must be able to inspect a `Result` as data.

```haskell
module ImportConfig (Seq :: ResultSequencing ConfigError) where
  -- Seq is the sequencing provider declared by this module's interface.
  loadConfig :: forall r. using (io :: Io r) =>
                Path ->{IO r, Async r, Cancel r, Diverge}
                  Result ConfigError Config
  loadConfig path = do
    bytes <- readConfigBytes path
    config <- parseConfig bytes
    pure config
```

Here the module parameter carries the designated sequencing-provider role in the signature. `readConfigBytes` reports `ConfigError`; its `Result` success payload becomes `bytes`. `parseConfig` is pure but returns the same error type. `pure` is the selected provider's ordinary operation. The compiler exposes the selected provider in diagnostics. There is no `Result.do` or other qualified-block requirement.

Outside a module selecting another provider, direct sequencing is the defined default. A generic function can require a sequencing dictionary in its `using` context; its elaborated body retains that dictionary when exported. Two active sequencing providers in the same selection scope are ambiguous unless explicitly bound through module wiring. No global instance priority or import-order tie-breaker changes block meaning.

Expected types constrain a selected provider and may infer its ordinary type parameters, such as `ConfigError`; they do not search noninjective associated families to guess control flow. Public signatures record the provider requirement when it is abstract. The details of the compiler-known provider role are part of the formal elaboration design, not an arbitrary convention that any module named `Seq` can exploit.

# Indexed sequencing and resource laws

A general monadic or stateful interpretation needs indexed action and result families so deferred effects cannot disappear. Its abstract shape is an indexed bind from an action with effects `e1` and a continuation producing an action with effects `e2` to a composed action accounting for both. The exact family may also index state transitions, resource ownership and failures. Ordinary direct expressions are reified into this representation only through the provider's checked elaboration interface.

It is unsound to use a naive unrestricted Haskell `Monad` dictionary that stores an effectful continuation in a supposedly pure value, duplicates a linear capture, or changes effect order without evidence. The initial compiler supports direct, `Result` and `Option` one-shot providers; arbitrary indexed providers require a specified and checked representation bridge before acceptance. This is an explicit implementation boundary, not a claim that all existing Haskell monads already fit.

For direct binding, `x <- rhs; rest` means execute `rhs`, bind its value and then execute `rest`. For the Result provider, it means execute `rhs`, return `Err e` on failure, or bind the `Ok` payload and execute `rest`. The compiler unions the effects of reachable computations conservatively; it can refine them only with checked evidence. `let` remains pure and strict in either interpretation. An unbound expression statement must satisfy the provider's discard/continuation rule. The final expression already has the provider's result shape; `pure` constructs that shape explicitly.

Monad identity and associativity laws are stated under an appropriate observational relation. They do not authorize arbitrary reordering, duplication, cancellation masking or omission of external effects. Effectful fusion rules must preserve the selected sequencing and cancellation contracts.

# Backend and compatibility consequences

Native backends may implement suspension using stackful tasks or transformed continuations. Wasm backends may lower to explicit state machines and WASI async calls without requiring Wasm stack switching. Runtime implementation choice is constrained by the same source effects and ownership contracts; it is not part of ordinary source function coloring.

An arbitrary blocking C call cannot become suspending by changing the `Io` dictionary. It needs an offload adapter, a genuinely asynchronous foreign API, or a declared blocking execution context. Foreign callbacks cannot unwind or suspend across an ABI that does not support that protocol.

Hot replacement checks runtime identity, handler contract, continuation representation, sequencing dictionary identity where specialized, and live registrations. Inlined sequencing operations and specialized runtime calls enter the dependent update set. Changing a scheduling policy can invalidate progress proofs even if all types are unchanged.

# Prior art and remaining formal work

[Zig 0.16's I/O interface](https://ziglang.org/download/0.16.0/release-notes.html) demonstrates explicitly passed I/O implementations. [Koka's effect handlers](https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html) demonstrate effect-based control abstractions. This proposal combines those inspirations with dependent modules, lexical evidence and ownership; it is not a statement that either language implements this exact design.

Required next formal results are effect preservation under handler lowering, safe one-shot continuation ownership, coherent dictionary elaboration, the indexed sequencing bridge, and a correspondence between runtime protocols and temporal models. Grammar checking alone establishes none of these.

[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

The initial compiler supports direct, `Result` and `Option` one-shot providers; arbitrary indexed providers require a specified and checked representation bridge before acceptance. For direct binding, `x <- rhs; rest` means execute `rhs`, bind its value and then execute `rest`. An unbound expression statement must satisfy the provider's discard/continuation rule. The final expression already has the provider's result shape; `pure` constructs that shape explicitly.

Monad identity and associativity laws are stated under an appropriate observational relation. They do not authorize arbitrary reordering, duplication, cancellation masking or omission of external effects. Effectful fusion rules must preserve the selected sequencing and cancellation contracts.

Native backends may implement suspension using stackful tasks or transformed continuations. Wasm backends may lower to explicit state machines and WASI async calls without requiring Wasm stack switching. Runtime implementation choice is constrained by the same source effects and ownership contracts; it is not part of ordinary source function coloring.

An arbitrary blocking C call cannot become suspending by changing the `Io` dictionary. It needs an offload adapter, a genuinely asynchronous foreign API, or a declared blocking execution context. Foreign callbacks cannot unwind or suspend across an ABI that does not support that protocol.

Hot replacement checks runtime identity, handler contract, continuation representation, sequencing dictionary identity where specialized, and live registrations. Learn the proposed notation by writing functions whose types describe their results. Prerequisite: ordinary functional programming. This is a design walkthrough, not an executable installation guide; the compiler and prelude do not yet exist.

# Start with strict functions

```haskell
twice :: Nat -> Nat
twice x = x + x

answer = twice 21
```

`answer` is `42`. `Nat` is an unbounded mathematical natural number in this draft. Function arguments are evaluated before the body. An explicitly pure arrow requires the compiler to justify termination; unsignatured local definitions may infer effects.

Use a machine integer type when bounded representation matters. Its checked addition returns an explicit overflow outcome; it does not silently inherit the semantics of `Nat`.

# Let a value appear in a type

```haskell
repeat :: forall a. using (copy :: Copy a) =>
          (n :: Nat) -> a -> Vec n a
repeat n x = case n of
  Zero -> Nil
  Succ k -> Cons x (repeat k x)
```

The constructor pattern `Succ k` matches a successor. The branches produce vectors of lengths `0` and `k + 1`. Recursion decreases `n`, so it is total. `Copy` is required because the element is reused.

`n` need not be a compile-time literal. A runtime input can determine the vector's length while the checker reasons symbolically about the relationship.

# Eliminate an impossible case

```haskell
first :: forall a n region. Ref region (Vec (n + 1) a) -> Ref region a
first xs = case xs of
  Cons x rest -> x
```

The implicit index `n` is universally quantified. `Nil` cannot have length `n + 1`, so it is impossible. The result borrows from the input, and the inferred lifetime prevents keeping the result after the input is destroyed.

Expected rejection:

```haskell
first Nil
```

There is no natural `n` satisfying `0 = n + 1`.

# Return a runtime witness

```haskell
pack :: forall a. List a -> Sigma (n :: Nat). Vec n a
pack xs = case xs of
  Nil -> (0, Nil)
  Cons x rest -> case pack rest of
    (n, tail) -> (n + 1, Cons x tail)
```

The dependent pair binds the returned length in the vector's type. The implementation must retain that length if later code reads it; dependent indices are not automatically erased.

# Exercise and answer

What should `zipExact` accept? Use two vectors with the same index:

```haskell
zipExact :: forall a b n. Vec n a -> Vec n b -> Vec n (a, b)
```

Its recursive implementation needs only the two matching constructor cases. A pair with unequal lengths is rejected at the call site or must first pass a runtime length-equality decision.

pages.markdown:
[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn how static evidence, runtime decisions, and unfinished proofs differ. Prerequisite: Tutorial 1. The examples use proposed prelude operations with the contracts described here.

# Build a bounded index

`Fin n` contains a natural number `i` and erased evidence that `i < n`. Its constructor is available only when that evidence exists.

```haskell
checkedIndex :: (n :: Nat) -> Nat -> Option (Fin n)
checkedIndex n i = case decide (i < n) of
  Yes bound -> Some (Fin i bound)
  No _ -> None
```

`decide` uses a total decision procedure for natural-number comparison. The successful result carries evidence about this particular `i` and `n`. It does not prove that all caller-supplied indices are valid.

```haskell
tryGet :: forall a n region. using (copy :: Copy a) =>
          Ref region (Vec n a) -> Nat -> Option a
tryGet xs i = case checkedIndex n i of
  Some index -> Some (Vec.getCopy xs index)
  None -> None
```

Here the length is available from the vector representation or a retained index. `Vec.getCopy` requires `Fin n` and returns the element without a bounds-error path. `tryGet` exposes invalid input as `None`.

# Prove a general statement

```haskell
proof plusZero :: (n :: Nat) -> Eq (n + 0) n
proof plusZero n = case n of
  Zero -> refl
  Succ k -> congr Succ (plusZero k)
```

This example uses addition defined recursively on its first argument. `refl` proves definitional equality. `congr` transports equality through a total function. The recursive proof is smaller because it uses `k`.

Proof execution is erased. Its recursive structure is checked before erasure, so infinite recursion cannot be used to manufacture evidence.

# Strengthen an interface gradually

A function initially returning `List a` can later return a package proving its result is sorted and a permutation of the input. Existing weaker code may still use the list projection. Code relying on sorting must request the stronger package from the beginning.

The compiler cannot silently upgrade the original return type because tests passed. Nor can it reinterpret a proof-search timeout as success.

# Diagnose three different failures

| Situation | Required response |
| --- | --- |
| `Fin(7, proof)` for a bound of `3` | Refute the obligation or report a concrete contradiction |
| A valid theorem exceeds the automation budget | Report unresolved evidence and allow an explicit lemma |
| A runtime index is unknown statically | Use a decision procedure and handle its failure branch |

An editor hole such as `?bound` can show the current context, but it cannot appear in an accepted artifact whose contract requires that proof.

# Exercise and answer

Can `decide(eventuallyResponds(server))` prove liveness at startup? No general decision procedure exists for that claim. Use a static temporal argument with explicit environment assumptions, or expose a bounded timeout outcome without calling it a proof of eventual response.

Next: Tutorial 3 explains how mutation and effects constrain evidence.

[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn how ownership protects both memory and facts about mutable state. Prerequisite: Tutorials 1 and 2. Borrow and resource syntax is provisional.

# Borrow instead of duplicate

```haskell
swap :: forall a n region. Mut region (Vec n a)
     -> Fin n -> Fin n ->{State region} ()
swap xs i j = Vec.swap xs i j
```

`Vec.swap` exchanges elements without copying or discarding them. The exclusive borrow prevents incompatible aliases during mutation. The vector length stays `n`, so the index evidence remains valid. The library operation must justify the equal-index case; a caller cannot create two mutable references to the same element by pretending the indices differ.

# Mutable refinements have a lifetime

Consider the following intended rejection:

```haskell
-- Rejected: evidence describes the old buffer view.
do
  let evidence = decide (i < length buffer)
  truncate buffer 0
  getUsingOldProof buffer i evidence
```

The evidence refers to the earlier state. Either the borrow rules prevent truncation while a dependent view is live, or the state transition invalidates the fact. A proof about yesterday's length is not a present bounds guarantee.

# Effects follow higher-order code

```haskell
map :: forall a b e. (a ->{|e} b) -> List a ->{|e} List b
```

Mapping a pure callback stays pure. Mapping a callback that reads files carries I/O. The operation preserves its specified callback order; effect polymorphism does not imply that callbacks commute.

A capability such as `FileReadCap` determines which reads are permitted. The `IO` effect only says that I/O may happen. Pure code cannot access an ambient network client without an effectful interface and the necessary authority.

# Acquire a resource in a scope

```haskell
loadText :: forall region. Ref region FileReadCap -> Path
         ->{IO, Diverge} Result ReadError String
loadText cap path = withFile cap path (\file -> File.readText file)
```

The proposed `withFile` combinator owns the handle and lends it to the callback. Its library contract defines cleanup on return, read failure, and supported cancellation paths. A process crash or a failed operating-system close needs the separately stated runtime policy.

Expected rejection: return a closure that captures `file` and can be called after `withFile` exits. The closure's borrow would outlive the handle.

# Exercise and answer

Can a multi-shot effect handler resume a continuation twice if it captured an owned transaction? Not without a valid duplication protocol. The ordinary continuation must be one-shot. Copyable captures permit more freedom; linear captures do not.

Next: Tutorial 4 packages operations and their laws into reusable modules.

pages.markdown:
[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn how one operation name can support several abstractions without erasing their differences. Prerequisite: dependent types, proofs, and effects from Tutorials 1 through 3.

# Package an operation and its model

For a reusable pure finite sequence, start with:

```haskell
signature FiniteSequence (c :: Type -> Type) where
  spec contents :: forall a. c a -> List a
  filter :: forall a. (a -> Bool) -> c a -> c a
  proof filterCorrect :: forall a. (p :: a -> Bool) -> (xs :: c a)
                      -> Eq (contents (filter p xs))
                            (List.filter p (contents xs))
```

The law says exactly which elements remain, including order and multiplicity. `contents` is a mathematical view; runtime code does not allocate that list just because a proof mentions it. This simplified interface assumes reusable immutable inputs. A resource-owning implementation needs a contract over views and ownership transfer.

# Choose a dictionary

```haskell
keepPositive :: forall c. using (sequence :: FiniteSequence c) => c Int -> c Int
keepPositive xs = sequence.filter (\x -> x > 0) xs
```

Callers can supply `PackedSequence` or `LinkedSequence` explicitly. An unambiguous implicit dictionary permits the shorter call. Laws are tied to that dictionary; a theorem about one equality or ordering implementation cannot justify an optimization using another.

# Allow the result type to change

Vectors need a more dependent signature:

```haskell
filterVec :: forall a n region. using (copy :: Copy a) =>
             (a -> Bool) -> Ref region (Vec n a)
             -> Sigma (m :: Nat). (Vec m a, Proof (m <= n))
```

`Proof` denotes an erased wrapper here. A complete correctness contract also establishes that the output equals the accepted subsequence. The size bound alone would allow an incorrect implementation that always returns the empty vector.

A general `Filtering` dictionary can supply an associated output family indexed by predicate and input view. Generic clients must additionally request the observation and laws they need; an arbitrary output family offers little useful reasoning by itself.

# Keep stream guarantees distinct

`filter` on a productive stream returns a search process unless there is evidence supporting total next-match search. A richer module can provide productive filtering when such evidence is supplied. An effectful source additionally specifies effect order, early termination, and cleanup.

These interfaces can share names and combinators while exposing different types. Implicit resolution should not silently switch between runtime algorithms based on a newly available proof.

# Exercise and answer

Would `all(output, p)` be a sufficient filter law? No. Returning nothing satisfies it. Require the exact accepted subsequence, or an equivalent combination of preservation, completeness, order, and multiplicity properties.

Next: Tutorial 5 constructs and proves properties of infinite streams.

Learn to distinguish productive infinite data from computations that may search forever. Prerequisite: Tutorials 1 through 4. Guarded syntax is provisional; the exact clock or size discipline remains an open foundation choice.

# Define a productive stream

```haskell
codata Stream (a :: Type) where
  head :: a
  tail :: Later (Stream a)

corec from :: Nat -> Stream Nat
corec from n = Stream { head = n, tail = delay (\() -> from (n + 1)) }
```

Producing the current head takes finite work. The recursive call is protected by `delay`, so requesting a finite prefix does not evaluate the entire infinite stream. `Later` is checked guarded delay, not a way to label arbitrary nontermination productive.

# Map without losing productivity

```haskell
corec map :: forall a b. (a -> b) -> Stream a -> Stream b
corec map f xs = Stream
  { head = f xs.head
  , tail = delay (\() -> map f (force xs.tail)) }
```

The callback is total and pure. The use of `force` occurs under the permitted delayed observation. A callback that diverges on a head cannot meet this type.

# Prove a fusion law by bisimulation

To establish `map(f, map(g, xs)) ≈ map(f ∘ g, xs)`, relate each pair with that form. Both heads reduce to `f(g(xs.head))`. Their tails have the same relationship after one permitted observation.

This establishes stream bisimilarity. The optimizer must use the associated congruence theorem for permitted contexts; the language does not automatically identify every bisimulation proof with definitional equality.

# See why filter differs

```haskell
filter (\x -> x % 2 == 0) (repeatForever 1)
```

No output element exists. A function accepting arbitrary predicates therefore cannot promise `Stream a`. It can return a `Process a` whose next output may require unbounded search.

For productive filtering, supply computational evidence sufficient to find the next match after each output. One strong approach is a total search operation returning a finite offset, proof of a match there, and proof that earlier elements were rejected. Another is a certified search driven by a retained bound. A merely erased classical existence assertion does not supply executable search.

Knowing a match occurs within each window can establish productivity, but implementing exact filtering must still preserve all matching elements and their order.

# Exercise and answer

pages.markdown:
[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn how to specify a service that intentionally runs forever. Prerequisite: Tutorial 5. Temporal formulas are specification notation; they are not runtime assertions that can inspect an infinite future.

# Give requests identities

Imagine a worker that accepts jobs and eventually records an outcome. Track each job by `JobId`, with states such as `Queued`, `Running`, `Succeeded`, and `Failed`. Keep completed-job history if the protocol uses it to prevent duplicate completion.

An abstract model might have transitions `Accept(id)`, `Start(id)`, and `Finish(id, outcome)`. The state invariant says a job has one status and cannot move back from a terminal status to `Running`.

Prove the invariant by checking the initial state and each transition. That inductive proof covers all reachable states even though the service can execute infinitely many transitions.

# State safety and progress separately

```haskell
always (completionCount requestId <= 1)
always (implies (accepted requestId) (eventually (completed requestId)))
```

The first formula forbids duplicate completion records. The second promises eventual completion for every accepted job. To establish the second, the protocol needs assumptions such as eventual scheduling, terminating job execution or a specified timeout outcome, and recoverable dependency behavior.

A job that is permanently disabled is not rescued by weak fairness. Weak fairness requires an action that remains enabled to eventually execute; strong fairness concerns actions enabled repeatedly. Choose the actual needed assumption rather than adding fairness as an unexplained label.

# Connect the implementation

Define a relation from concrete worker state to the abstract model: queue entries map to `Queued`, owned work items map to `Running`, and durable outcomes map to terminal states. Each executable operation must correspond to an allowed abstract transition or a justified internal step.

For liveness, internal steps cannot stutter forever while a response obligation is pending. A progress measure and scheduler assumptions must connect implementation execution to the temporal theorem.

# Preserve uncertainty at external boundaries

A timeout after submitting a payment may mean the payment failed, succeeded, or remains pending. The state machine should contain an unknown-outcome state and a reconciliation transition if the external protocol requires them. Returning `Failed` merely because the local socket timed out can violate the intended contract.

The same issue matters during hot replacement: the new version must inherit pending and unknown outcomes, not just the successful records.

# Exercise and answer

If a model checker explores ten jobs and all allowed queue states under that limit, has it proved the unbounded implementation correct? No. That result covers the modeled instance. A parameterized proof or a justified abstraction theorem is needed to extend it.

Next: Tutorial 7 turns semantic laws into executable optimization rules.

pages.title: Tutorial 7 Rewrites and stream fusion
pages.markdown:
[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn to register an optimization only after establishing the law it needs. Prerequisite: modules and stream reasoning from Tutorials 4 and 5.

# Begin with a pure law

For finite lists and total pure reusable callbacks:

```haskell
proof mapFusion :: (f :: Int -> Int) -> (g :: Int -> Int)
                -> (xs :: List Int)
                -> Eq (List.map f (List.map g xs))
                      (List.map (\x -> f (g x)) xs)
proof mapFusion f g xs = case xs of
  Nil -> refl
  Cons x rest -> congr (\ys -> Cons (f (g x)) ys) (mapFusion f g rest)
```

The proof uses the recursive definition of `List.map` and induction on the finite list. Mathematical `Int` avoids overflow ambiguity. This law is about pure finite values under the draft's idealized resource semantics; it does not promise identical allocation behavior or out-of-memory outcomes.

# Register the direction

```haskell
rewrite mapMap forall (f :: Int -> Int) (g :: Int -> Int)
                     (xs :: List Int). where
  match List.map f (List.map g xs)
  replace List.map (\x -> f (g x)) xs
  justify mapFusion f g xs
```

The theorem establishes validity. The rewrite declaration selects a direction. A phase or cost policy decides when to use it. The compiler checks applicability, including the callback types, and limits optimization work to avoid cyclic rewriting.

This rule does not become a new definitional equality in the type checker.

# Lower a producer pipeline

```haskell
sumSquares :: forall n region. Ref region (Vec n Nat) -> Nat
sumSquares xs = Stream.fold 0 (+)
  (Stream.map (\x -> x * x) (Vec.stream xs))
```

Here `stream()` borrows the vector and yields copied natural values. Its finite producer contract guarantees `n` elements. A lowering can specialize the producer state machine to a loop with an accumulator, eliminating intermediate collection materialization.

The compiler may still allocate for mathematical integers. A no-intermediate-collections assertion does not mean zero allocation.

# Reject an invalid extension

Replacing the callbacks with logging functions changes the question. In strict eager lists, nested maps log all inner calls before outer calls. A fused loop interleaves them. The pure theorem cannot justify that transformation.

An explicit effectful stream pipeline already has a specified stepping order, so a different theorem may justify eliminating its machinery while preserving that order.

# Inspect the result

A proposed optimization report should show the rule used, its law identity, any remaining producer allocation, and the location that blocked specialization. If code is imported as replaceable, the compiler must preserve its dispatch boundary unless it records the specialization dependency required for future updates.

# Exercise and answer

Can a proof of real-number associativity justify reassociating floating-point addition? No. Use the machine semantics, or require an explicitly selected approximate relation with a proved error bound.

Next: Tutorial 8 generates definitions and proofs at compile time.

# Platform specialization

A fused producer loop can be specialized again using target-indexed laws. The next proof must cover machine lane arithmetic, memory access, tails, and capability-scoped dispatch. A correct fusion theorem alone does not justify vectorization. Tutorial 10 develops a wrapping-integer reduction with a scalar fallback.

pages.markdown:
[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn to combine hygienic typed code generation with real compile-time I/O. Prerequisite: dependent modules and effects. The database and generator APIs here are proposed interfaces, not connections to an actual database.

# Construct typed code

```haskell
stage addOne :: Code Nat -> Code Nat
stage addOne body = [| let x = $(body) in x + 1 |]
```

The generated `x` is a fresh binding. A caller's `x` inside spliced syntax keeps its original identity. A macro helper resolves where the macro was defined. Intentional capture requires an explicit operation.

`Code<Nat>` abbreviates closed, pure code at the target stage. Open code, effects, and captured resources require richer inferred context information.

# Export a generator

```haskell
module SchemaBindings where
  stage derive :: SchemaSnapshot -> Declarations
  stage derive schema = CodecGenerator.derive schema

module Client where
  import stage SchemaBindings
```

The compiled module exports executable generator code and permitted reflection metadata. A generator may also be used in its defining module when the dependency graph allows it. It cannot inspect private representation just because it runs during compilation.

# Read the real schema

```haskell
generate do
  snapshot <- Stage.snapshot "billing-schema" (\io ->
    Stage.withDatabase io (secret "SCHEMA_DATABASE_URL") ReadSchema
      (\db -> introspectConsistently db))
  emit (SchemaBindings.derive snapshot)
```

The snapshot helper interprets the current build mode. Refresh executes the callback and captures the schema. Replay uses the recorded snapshot and does not connect. Live executes the external read and records the provenance without pretending an old cached answer is current.

`withDatabase` scopes the compile-time connection. Its handle is not embedded in generated runtime code. The secret authorizes access and is omitted from generated source and ordinary snapshots. Schema content may still be sensitive and needs the chosen recording policy.

# Check generated evidence

The generator can emit row types, typed queries, codecs, and proofs relative to the captured schema. Every declaration goes through normal elaboration and proof checking. A generator's claim that a decoder is total is not itself evidence.

At runtime, a proposed `connect` operation validates the expected compatibility and returns `Connection s` only on success. A migration epoch, lease, or equivalent deployment policy must maintain relevant schema facts after validation. A startup check cannot prevent an independent administrator from changing the database later.

# Diagnose a staging cycle

If `derive` needs the definition of `GeneratedRow` to compile, but executing `derive` is what creates `GeneratedRow`, the compiler reports that dependency cycle. Moving files cannot make the logical dependency disappear.

# Exercise and answer

May a generator invoke a subprocess to read a schema file? Yes, with a subprocess capability. Reproducible replay must capture the relevant input, tool identity, and configuration. Host pointers or unrecorded environment state cannot become portable target constants.

Next: Tutorial 9 packages a compatible live upgrade.

pages.title: Tutorial 9 Compatible hot upgrades
pages.markdown:
[Documentation overview](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b647a1112d5c8191a20ef25f039a366a)

Learn to evolve module state without changing what existing clients are promised. Prerequisite: ownership, contracts, temporal reasoning, and compilation dependencies from earlier tutorials.

# Start with a simple contract

A counter exposes `read` and `increment`. Its observable model is a natural-number total. Version 1 stores one value:

```haskell
record StateV1 where
  value :: Nat
```

Version 2 separates a base and an accumulated delta:

```haskell
record StateV2 where
  base :: Nat
  delta :: Nat
```

Its read operation returns `base + delta`; increment increases `delta` by one. The external contract remains the same.

# Define the migration relation

```haskell
spec related :: StateV1 -> StateV2 -> Prop
spec related old next = Eq old.value (next.base + next.delta)

migrate :: StateV1 %1 -> StateV2
migrate old = StateV2 { base = old.value, delta = 0 }
```

The migration theorem follows from addition's zero law. Increment preservation uses the natural-number arithmetic law relating `base + (delta + 1)` to `(base + delta) + 1`.

These proofs establish the chosen counter model. They do not automatically establish concurrent atomicity, bounded memory, or latency. Those properties would need their own contracts.

# Choose drain and replace

For this example, pause new calls, wait for active calls to finish, and acquire exclusive state ownership. The runtime then migrates the state and publishes the new dispatch epoch. No borrowed pointer into `StateV1` may survive the layout change.

If an active call never finishes, the runtime cannot claim quiescence. It may reject the update or use an explicitly justified cancellation protocol.

# Package evidence and operational requirements

```haskell
upgrade CounterV1 to CounterV2 where
  strategy = DrainAndReplace
  stateMigration = migrate
  relation = related
  evidence = CounterUpgradeProofs
```

`CounterUpgradeProofs` is a required module containing invariant, operation-refinement, and resource-transfer evidence. This declaration is a package sketch; it is not a complete proof merely because the field has a name.

The runtime additionally checks artifact identities, old-version matches, safe-point conditions, and dependency completeness. Static evidence establishes what transitions are valid; coordination establishes that the actual process can take one now.

# Account for specialization

Clients using `import replaceable Counter` call through the stable boundary. A client that specialized or inlined version 1 may need replacement too. The dependency manifest identifies that client; updating a symbol does not rewrite its existing machine code.

Old code stays loaded while any old closure, callback, frame, or destructor still requires it. Rollback requires a valid reverse transition if the state has already changed.

# Exercise and answer

Can the same pattern replace a worker with pending external payments? Only with a richer relation preserving request identities, pending work, unknown outcomes, and temporal obligations. Copying successful records and dropping the rest is incompatible even if the exported function types match.

Next: Tutorial 10 adds target-specific proofs and SIMD rules, including their interaction with hot replacement. The Example catalogue and Open decisions collect conformance cases and implementation priorities.

pages.title: Tutorial 11 Foreign libraries
pages.markdown:
Use an existing native library through a small, explicit boundary. This tutorial uses a fictional C codec API; the syntax and wrapper APIs are proposals.

# Start with the public contract

The application should see an owned decoder and a typed result, rather than pointers and integer status codes.

```haskell
decode :: forall region. Mut region Decoder -> Ref region Bytes
       -> (limit :: Nat) ->{Foreign Codec, Blocking, Diverge}
          Result DecodeError (BoundedBytes limit)
```

`BoundedBytes limit` contains bytes together with evidence that their length is at most `limit`. This says nothing yet about whether the bytes are a correct decompression. A stronger interface can add that semantic relationship when evidence or an explicitly accepted assumption supports it.

The effect signature records that the call crosses into foreign code, may block, and may fail to terminate. `Result` records ordinary reported errors. A crash or undefined behavior inside an unverified native library does not become a recoverable `Err` merely because the wrapper returns `Result`.

# Describe the raw ABI separately

The raw declaration must specify the calling convention, integer widths, pointer validity, output initialization and allocator pairing. The wrapper must establish the input preconditions and interpret successful outputs according to the foreign contract.

For this codec, the assumed contract is: input and output pointers are used only during the call; the codec never writes beyond the supplied capacity; success initializes exactly the reported prefix; and destruction must use the codec's own close operation. These are reviewable assumptions unless proved against the linked implementation.

The wrapper allocates storage, lends it exclusively, calls the decoder, checks the status and reported length, and exposes only the initialized prefix. A successful length check establishes the returned length bound. It does **not** establish that the callee avoided an earlier out-of-bounds write. A safe public wrapper over native code is therefore conditional on the foreign implementation meeting its safety contract.

# Choose the trust profile

The build can accept an audited native codec, require a verified implementation with matching artifact evidence, or call an isolated worker/component whose outputs are validated. Isolation changes the failure boundary; it does not prove that decoded content is semantically correct. The manifest records which profile the application chose and its transitive dependencies.

Generated declarations help with layout and naming. They cannot infer a correct ownership or threading contract from a C header alone.

# Handle blocking and cancellation

Put blocking work on an executor that supports it. Move an owned input buffer into the operation, or keep its borrow alive until completion. If the task receives cancellation while the C function is running, the runtime requests cancellation if supported and waits for the protocol's completion acknowledgment before releasing memory. A timeout is not acknowledgment.

Callbacks need a stable trampoline and a registration resource. Closing that resource must establish that no future or in-flight callback can use its context. When that context refers to replaceable code, the old code stays resident until registration and execution have both ended.

# Check your understanding

Would changing the result type to `Result<DecodeError, Bytes>` remove the need to trust the native library's memory behavior? No: weakening the result contract removes a length theorem, not the pointer and lifetime obligations. To reduce that trust, change the implementation evidence or isolation boundary.

See the foreign interface specification for layouts, callbacks, unwinding, linkage and deployment policy. The source example is `examples/09-foreign-codec.lang`.

pages.title: Tutorial 12 WebAssembly components
pages.markdown:
Export a library as a Wasm component while keeping its stronger source-language contracts visible inside the program. This tutorial uses a portable, synchronous WIT interface; async APIs can be added with the WASI 0.3 profile.

# Define the interoperable shape

```wit
package example:codec@0.1.0;

interface decoder {
  enum decode-error { malformed, too-large }
  decode: func(input: list<u8>, limit: u32)
    -> result<list<u8>, decode-error>;
}

world codec-plugin {
  export decoder;
}
```

WIT describes the values and interfaces that another language can call. It does not express the dependent claim that the returned list has length at most `limit`, nor that it decodes the input correctly. Our generated source signature can expose a stronger result when the local implementation proves it.

# Generate and check an adapter

On export, the adapter translates the checked source result into canonical component values. On import from an arbitrary component, it starts with the weaker WIT result. It checks the length before constructing `BoundedBytes limit` and returns an additional boundary error if validation fails.

The adapter must also establish integer conversions, string or list representation, resource ownership and cleanup. Proof terms are erased; essential runtime tags, lengths and discriminants remain. Passing a dependent value does not imply sending its proof object over the ABI.

The isolated implementation may trap or terminate without producing a result. Treat those outcomes according to the host's component-failure policy. A valid length is evidence about that returned value, not a proof that the external implementation is correct on all inputs.

# Choose a target and capabilities

Use the WASI 0.3 component profile for hosts supporting that interface set. Keep a pinned WASI 0.2 profile where compatibility is needed. For a browser, generate the selected component or core-module JavaScript adapter and request the corresponding host interfaces explicitly. Browser DOM access is a host binding, not an automatic WASI facility.

Wasm itself does not grant filesystem or network access. The component's world declares imports; the application supplies only the selected capabilities. A decoder needing no I/O should have no filesystem or network imports. Build-time schema generation has a separate capability environment from runtime execution.

# Add async deliberately

A WASI future can represent an eventual outcome; a WASI stream transports a sequence with host protocol rules. Neither is automatically our productive infinite `Stream a`. An adapter must account for end-of-stream, errors, cancellation and the separate completion outcome where the interface has one.

For a bounded consumer, backpressure is part of the contract. A cancelled consumer must release its registration or keep it alive until the host acknowledges completion. Async I/O can work on a single-thread event loop; parallel CPU work additionally requires a supported execution capability.

# Add SIMD and hot replacement

Ship a portable module and a SIMD-enabled variant when host support differs. Choose a valid variant before instantiation: placing unsupported Wasm instructions behind a runtime branch may still make the entire module fail validation.

Hot replacement happens through runtime-managed dispatch and resource migration. An old component resource cannot be reinterpreted as a handle owned by a new instance. Drain, translate, or retain it according to the upgrade package, including outstanding async operations.

The accompanying files are `examples/10-wasm-component.lang` and `examples/codec.wit`. See the WebAssembly and WASI specification for the full backend requirements.
