pages.title: Tutorial 13 Structured concurrency
pages.markdown:
Run two independent operations concurrently while keeping ownership and failure behavior visible. Concurrency is part of the effectful program layer; it does not weaken the total logical fragment used to check proofs.

# Give tasks a scope

```haskell
loadPair :: forall r. using (io :: Io r) =>
            Request -> Request
            ->{Async r, IO r, Cancel r, Diverge}
              Result LoadError (Bytes, Bytes)
loadPair left right = withScope $ \s -> do
  a <- spawn s (\() -> fetch left)
  b <- spawn s (\() -> fetch right)
  joinAllOrCancel s a b
```

These are proposed APIs. Each child owns its request. `joinAllOrCancel` returns both successful results or follows its documented error policy: request cancellation of the remaining work, wait for cleanup, then return an error. The `LoadError` contract includes supported task failures and cancellation. A child that cannot stop may prevent the scope from returning; the type does not claim bounded shutdown.

Scoped borrows are also useful: tasks can borrow input when the scope proves that no task outlives it. Capturing an exclusive borrow in two simultaneously live tasks is rejected unless a safe partition or synchronization abstraction justifies it. For work that may migrate between threads, captured values and results need transfer evidence.

# Treat cancellation as a protocol

Consider a task calling a native decoder. Receiving cancellation does not make the C stack disappear. The task retains its output buffer and module reference until the operation finishes or acknowledges that it will no longer access them.

The same issue occurs with asynchronous hosts. Cancellation requested, cancellation observed and cleanup completed are distinct events. A timeout can report that the caller stopped waiting, but an API must explain who now owns the unfinished work and its resources.

# Use bounded channels for pipelines

A channel carries owned messages and has an explicit capacity. A successful send transfers ownership to the channel or receiver. A send cancelled before its commit point returns the message; cancellation after commit cannot give the same ownership back to the sender.

This makes bounded producer/consumer pipelines natural. Backpressure limits queued messages, although it does not bound every allocation in the application. Closing an endpoint must specify what happens to queued messages and blocked peers. An actor can package state, a mailbox and its handler behind a module interface.

# Compose shared-state operations

For a Haskell-like alternative to manual locking, the proposed STM library permits atomic transactions over transactional cells. Its effect restriction forbids ordinary I/O, FFI and async suspension in a retryable transaction. A transaction can execute repeatedly before committing, so performing a payment or closing an external handle inside it would be unsound.

Use a post-commit protocol for external effects, with durable records when crash recovery matters. Atomic memory updates alone do not make a remote action exactly once.

# State the proof you actually need

Ownership can establish the absence of data races. A channel law can establish message ownership transfer. A lock-order argument can exclude certain deadlocks. A temporal theorem can establish eventual response under explicit scheduler and environment assumptions. These are different results.

Test cancellation at suspension points and explore schedules to find counterexamples. Record the explored bounds. Successful tests do not become a universal liveness proof.

During hot replacement, drain or migrate the scope's children, mailboxes, callbacks and pending host operations as well as the module's visible state. A quiescent exported function stack alone is insufficient.

See `examples/11-structured-tasks.lang` and the concurrency specification for scheduler capabilities, atomics, supervision and upgrade rules.

pages.title: Tutorial 14 Haskell-like syntax, effects and runtime selection
pages.markdown:
The current notation is strict and Haskell-like. Types use `::`, definitions use equations, calls use whitespace, and indentation groups declarations and statements. `twice 21` evaluates to 42; `twice` can be defined by `twice x = x + x`.

# Bind a value or sequence an operation

```haskell
checkedIndex :: (n :: Nat) -> Nat -> Option (Fin n)
checkedIndex n i = case decide (i < n) of
  Yes bound -> Some (Fin i bound)
  No _      -> None
```

The first parameter appears in the result type. A successful decision supplies proof evidence for the concrete bound; the compiler may erase the proof but must retain the comparison. A failed check produces `None`.

In ordinary direct `do`, `<-` sequences a computation and binds its whole result. If a read returns `Result ReadError Bytes`, the binding receives that Result; use `case` to inspect it. `let` is reserved for pure bindings, even though both forms are strict.

# Spawn work explicitly

```haskell
loadPair :: forall r. using (io :: Io r) =>
            Request -> Request
            ->{Async r, IO r, Cancel r, Diverge}
              Result LoadError (Bytes, Bytes)
loadPair left right = withScope $ \s -> do
  a <- spawn s (\() -> fetch left)
  b <- spawn s (\() -> fetch right)
  joinAllOrCancel s a b
```

The lambdas delay the calls until the tasks run. Without them, strict argument evaluation would execute a call before passing its result to spawn. Ordinary suspension needs no `await`: the effect row already records it. Spawning creates explicit child tasks, while ordinary calls sequence within the current task.

The scope retains children and their resource obligations until joined. Cancelling one child does not prove its foreign call has stopped. The exposed divergence effect also prevents this function from being used as a total logical proof.

# Select an implementation

# Bounded indexing

`checkedIndex(3, 2)` returns an index usable with a vector of length three. `checkedIndex(3, 3)` returns `None`. A successful runtime comparison creates evidence about the concrete value; that evidence is erased, while the comparison remains where static proof is unavailable.

For pure total functions, the list induction supplies a proof of the map-composition equation. The rewrite uses that exact theorem. The intended optimization removes an intermediate list under the selected pure semantic model.

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Proposed prelude and borrow-pattern rules; not compiled.
module BoundedIndex where
  checkedIndex :: (n :: Nat) -> Nat -> Option (Fin n)
  checkedIndex n i = case decide (i < n) of
    Yes bound -> Some (Fin i bound)
    No _ -> None

            Ref region (Vec n a) -> Nat -> Option a

    Some index -> Some (Vec.getCopy xs index)
    None -> None
```

## Vector filtering

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Algorithm; additional sequence laws are proof targets.
module VectorFilter where
  filter :: forall a n region. using (copy :: Copy a) =>
            (a -> Bool) -> Ref region (Vec n a)
            -> Sigma (m :: Nat). Vec m a
  filter predicate xs = case xs of
    Nil -> (0, Nil)
    Cons x rest ->
      let keep = predicate (copyOut x)
          packed = filter predicate rest
      in case packed of
        (m, tail) -> if keep
          then (m + 1, Cons (copyOut x) tail)
          else (m, tail)

  -- Strict let preserves source predicate order.
  -- Borrow matching yields references; copyOut requires Copy evidence.
  -- Prove by induction: m <= n and exact predicate-selected subsequence.
  -- The result retains the witness m, not just an erased proof of existence.
```

## Map fusion

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Pure finite reusable lists and total callbacks.
module PureMapFusion where
  proof mapFusion :: (f :: Int -> Int) -> (g :: Int -> Int)
                  -> (xs :: List Int)
                  -> Eq (List.map f (List.map g xs))
                        (List.map (\x -> f (g x)) xs)
  proof mapFusion f g xs = case xs of
    Nil -> refl
    Cons x rest ->
      congr (\ys -> Cons (f (g x)) ys) (mapFusion f g rest)

  rewrite mapMap forall (f :: Int -> Int) (g :: Int -> Int)
                       (xs :: List Int). where
    match List.map f (List.map g xs)
    replace List.map (\x -> f (g x)) xs
    justify mapFusion f g xs

  -- This theorem does not allow effectful callbacks or extend definitional equality.
```

## Productive streams

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. The guarded Later calculus still needs a formal choice.
module NaturalStreams where
  codata Stream (a :: Type) where
    head :: a
    tail :: Later (Stream a)

  corec from :: Nat -> Stream Nat
  corec from n = Stream { head = n, tail = delay (\() -> from (n + 1)) }

  corec map :: forall a b. (a -> b) -> Stream a -> Stream b
  corec map f xs = Stream
    { head = f xs.head
    , tail = delay (\() -> map f (force xs.tail)) }

  -- Finite observations of map (\x -> x * x) (from 0): 0, 1, 4, 9, ...

  -- Arbitrary filtering remains a process without recurring-match evidence.
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. State model, not a complete deployable package.
module CounterEvolution where
  record StateV1 where
    value :: Nat
  record StateV2 where
    base :: Nat
    delta :: Nat

  viewV1 :: StateV1 -> Nat
  viewV1 s = s.value
  viewV2 :: StateV2 -> Nat

  incrementV1 :: StateV1 %1 -> StateV1
```

```haskell
module PlatformSum where
  scalar :: forall n region. Ref region (Vec n U32) -> U32
  scalar xs = Stream.fold U32.zero U32.wrappingAdd (Vec.stream xs)

  target rewrite sumWrap32Vector
    forall t w n region (xs :: Ref region (Vec n U32)).
    using (vectors :: VecU32Target t w) where
    match scalar xs
    replace Simd.sumWrap32 vectors xs
    require Available vectors
    justify SumProofs.scalarToSimd vectors xs

    None -> scalar xs
```

```haskell
module CheckedComponentClient where
  record BoundedBytes (limit :: Nat) where
    bytes :: Bytes
    erased bound :: length bytes <= limit

  decode :: forall region. Ref region Bytes -> (limit :: U32)
         ->{Foreign Component, Diverge}
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Algorithm; additional sequence laws are proof targets.
module VectorFilter where
  filter :: forall a n region. using (copy :: Copy a) =>
            (a -> Bool) -> Ref region (Vec n a)
            -> Sigma (m :: Nat). Vec m a
  filter predicate xs = case xs of
    Nil -> (0, Nil)
    Cons x rest ->
      let keep = predicate (copyOut x)
          packed = filter predicate rest
      in case packed of
        (m, tail) -> if keep
          then (m + 1, Cons (copyOut x) tail)
          else (m, tail)

  -- Strict let preserves source predicate order.
  -- Borrow matching yields references; copyOut requires Copy evidence.
  -- Prove by induction: m <= n and exact predicate-selected subsequence.
  -- The result retains the witness m, not just an erased proof of existence.
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Pure finite reusable lists and total callbacks.
module PureMapFusion where
  proof mapFusion :: (f :: Int -> Int) -> (g :: Int -> Int)
                  -> (xs :: List Int)
                  -> Eq (List.map f (List.map g xs))
                        (List.map (\x -> f (g x)) xs)
  proof mapFusion f g xs = case xs of
    Nil -> refl
    Cons x rest ->
      congr (\ys -> Cons (f (g x)) ys) (mapFusion f g rest)

  rewrite mapMap forall (f :: Int -> Int) (g :: Int -> Int)
                       (xs :: List Int). where
    match List.map f (List.map g xs)
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. The guarded Later calculus still needs a formal choice.
module NaturalStreams where
  codata Stream (a :: Type) where
    head :: a
    tail :: Later (Stream a)

  corec from :: Nat -> Stream Nat
  corec from n = Stream { head = n, tail = delay (\() -> from (n + 1)) }

  corec map :: forall a b. (a -> b) -> Stream a -> Stream b
  corec map f xs = Stream
    { head = f xs.head
    , tail = delay (\() -> map f (force xs.tail)) }

  -- delay takes a checked guarded thunk; ordinary strict calls do not create delay.
  -- Finite observations of map (\x -> x * x) (from 0): 0, 1, 4, 9, ...
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. State model, not a complete deployable package.
module CounterEvolution where
  record StateV1 where
    value :: Nat
  record StateV2 where
    base :: Nat
    delta :: Nat

  viewV1 :: StateV1 -> Nat
  viewV1 s = s.value
  viewV2 :: StateV2 -> Nat
  viewV2 s = s.base + s.delta
```

```haskell
    opaque type Decoder :: Type

      bytes :: Bytes

  -- establish pointer access, interpret initialization, and check written <= limit.
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Adapter sketch for codec.wit; host failure policy is explicit.
module CheckedComponentClient where
  record BoundedBytes (limit :: Nat) where
    bytes :: Bytes
    erased bound :: length bytes <= limit

  decode :: forall region. Ref region Bytes -> (limit :: U32)
         ->{Foreign Component, Diverge}
           Result BoundaryError (BoundedBytes (toNat limit))
  decode input limit = do
    outcome <- Raw.decode input limit
    case outcome of
      Err e -> Err (ForeignError e)
      Ok bytes -> case decide (length bytes <= toNat limit) of
        Yes bound -> Ok (BoundedBytes { bytes = bytes, bound = bound })
        No _ -> Err ContractViolation

  -- Direct do binds the whole Result; it does not automatically short-circuit.
```

```haskell
-- Surface 0.2. Ordinary functions; no async/await function category.

              Request -> Request
              ->{Async r, IO r, Cancel r, Diverge}
                Result LoadError (Bytes, Bytes)

    a <- spawn s (\() -> fetch left)
    b <- spawn s (\() -> fetch right)
    joinAllOrCancel s a b
```

## Runtime effects and unqualified do
The effect-polymorphic traversal works with both pure and suspending callbacks. A separate module selects Result sequencing through its signature parameter; the source still uses ordinary `do`.

```haskell
  traverse :: forall a b e. (a ->{|e} b) -> List a ->{|e} List b

    Nil -> Nil
    Cons x rest -> do
      y <- f x
      ys <- traverse f rest
      pure (Cons y ys)

  -- Direct sequencing binds ordinary results; callbacks are reusable here.

                Path ->{IO r, Async r, Cancel r, Diverge}
                  Result ConfigError Config
  loadConfig path = do
    bytes <- readConfigBytes path
    config <- parseConfig bytes
    pure config

  -- io is a lexical runtime argument. Supplying it does not handle effects.
  -- An explicit call can use: loadConfig @{io = chosenIO} path

```

The language requirements are ambitious but coherent enough to define a research and implementation program. This page separates established goals from proposed mechanisms and unresolved semantic choices. No language name has been selected.

# Established requirements

- Strict functional execution with full dependent types from the core.

- Memory safety and explicit ownership of resources, with useful error and effect guarantees.

- Incremental verification without treating missing evidence as established truth.

- Haskell-like higher-order abstraction and TypeScript-like local narrowing and record ergonomics.

- Modules or typeclass-style abstraction that carry different result families, laws, and guarantees.

- Inductive, coinductive, and temporal reasoning, including infinite behavior.

- User-defined rewrite rules and stream fusion with appropriate correctness evidence.

- Platform-specific proof modules and SIMD rewrites with explicit target semantics, availability, and fallback policies.

- Hygienic, cross-module metaprogramming with fewer accidental staging restrictions.

- Compile-time file, subprocess, network, and database access.

- Compatible hot swapping across interfaces, state, resources, protocols, temporal properties, and compiled dependencies.

- FFI support for external libraries with explicit ownership, ABI, effect and trust boundaries.

- First-class Wasm/WASI deployment and a concurrency model that composes with proofs and hot replacement.

# Proposed mechanisms

| Proposal | Why it fits |
| --- | --- |
| Dependent modules with implicit dictionary arguments | Unifies explicit abstraction and typeclass ergonomics |
| A quantitative dependent foundation | Connects erasure and usage, while leaving borrowing to be modeled explicitly |
| Total logical fragment and effectful executable computations | Permits services without admitting divergent proofs |
| Explicit runtime decisions | Makes dynamic verification visible and predictable |
| Proof-carrying optimizer rules | Lets libraries provide checked specialization and fusion |
| Target-indexed proof modules | Shares algorithm proofs while exposing architecture-specific instruction and memory laws |
| Guarded codata plus separate processes | Separates productive data from unbounded search and waiting |
| Captured stage inputs and replay | Supports real external generation and reproducible builds |
| Checked upgrade packages with runtime safe points | Combines static compatibility with operational coordination |
| C ABI plus checked wrappers and explicit foreign assumptions | Practical native integration with reviewable trust |
| WASI 0.3 component profile with pinned 0.2 compatibility | Portable typed interfaces and async interoperability |
| Structured scopes, bounded channels and optional STM | Haskell-like composition with explicit lifetimes and cancellation |

# Decisions that need a formal design

| Question | Decision needed before |
| --- | --- |
| Universe hierarchy, equality, proof irrelevance and elimination | Kernel implementation |
| Resource usage algebra and dependent borrowing | Claiming memory and logical soundness together |
| Effect calculus and continuation multiplicity | General handlers and asynchronous APIs |
| Guarded recursion, clocks or sized types | Accepting productive codata and coinductive proofs |
| Immutable sharing and reclamation strategy | Stable runtime representation and performance claims |
| Abstract type identity and functor generativity | Separate compilation and module evolution |
| Optimization equivalence and observable allocation failure | Certifying transformations consistently |
| Typed-code contexts and stage dependencies | Hygienic dependent metaprogramming |
| Migration atomicity and cancellation semantics | Production hot replacement |
| Certificate formats and trusted backends | Meaningful artifact assurance profiles |
| Instruction models, target capability lifetime and scalable widths | Sound platform-specific SIMD specialization |
| Native pointer provenance, callback entry and unwind policy | Publishing safe foreign wrappers |
| Source concurrency memory model and backend correspondence | Claiming data-race freedom across native and Wasm |
| Cancellation, task failure and cleanup semantics | Stabilizing async APIs |
| Exact component profiles, host support and adapter rules | Declaring a supported Wasm deployment matrix |
| STM rollback ownership and scheduling assumptions | Claiming transactional and progress guarantees |

Syntax remains provisional. A concrete surface grammar is now specified in draft 0.2; the sound core calculus and elaboration judgments still require formalization. Surface convenience must elaborate to explicit core evidence; it cannot substitute for these decisions.

# Implementation milestones

1. **Define the core.** Specify universes, dependent functions and pairs, inductive families, equality, erasure, and totality. Implement a small checker and reference evaluator. Full dependent types are present from this milestone.

2. **Integrate resources and effects.** Formalize usage, borrows, ghost views, failure, and cancellation. Prove the relevant preservation and logical-soundness results for the selected subset.

3. **Add elaboration and modules.** Implement inference, narrowing, dependent records, dictionary resolution, opaque interfaces, and useful proof diagnostics.

4. **Add infinite behavior.** Implement guarded codata and its proof principles. Define process semantics and the bridge from executable code to temporal models.

5. **Add metaprogramming.** Implement hygienic expansion, typed quotations, stage dependency scheduling, capability-scoped I/O, captured inputs, and replay.

6. **Add checked optimization.** Begin with directed rules for a small pure IR, then stream fusion, effect-aware lowerings, target-specific SIMD rules, and dependency manifests. Expand only when preservation arguments exist.

7. **Add runtime evolution.** Begin with drain-and-replace for private module state. Then add coexistence and explicit continuation migration with their additional proofs.

Each milestone should run the relevant positive and negative cases in the example catalogue once an implementation exists. The milestones do not defer dependent types; they progressively establish the other features around a dependent foundation.

# Research risks to resolve early

The most difficult interfaces are dependent types with mutable ownership, erased logic with executable witnesses, coinduction with effects, and optimization dependencies with live replacement. A prototype that treats these as unrelated plugins would miss the core design problem.

The initial deliverable should be a small coherent calculus and a few complete end-to-end examples, including a checked vector operation, a productive stream law, a generated schema interface, and a stateful upgrade. A large syntax surface without those examples would provide little evidence that the design works.

# Backend and concurrency implementation track

Alongside the core milestones, implement a small C ABI wrapper layer, a portable core-Wasm backend and WIT adapters. Begin concurrency with local structured scopes, cooperative cancellation, bounded channels and explicit blocking-call handling. Establish the source memory model before adding migratable tasks, atomics or claims about shared-memory execution.

Use an isolated codec component and a scoped two-request client as early integration examples. Test ownership at cancellation races, foreign callback draining, component trap handling, cross-target widths and Wasm feature selection. Extend the hot-upgrade milestone to these resources before adding arbitrary continuation migration. STM and advanced session or lock-free libraries remain later work built on the checked foundations.

# Draft 0.2 syntax and runtime decisions

Adopt a strict Haskell-like surface with unqualified module/typeclass-driven `do`. Suspension is an effect of ordinary functions, with lexical runtime capabilities passed explicitly in the core. The published EBNF fixes concrete syntax; the formal elaboration, handler ownership and indexed sequencing bridge remain proof and implementation work. Initial sequencing providers are direct, Result and Option. Arbitrary indexed providers require the checked bridge described in [Runtime capabilities, effects and sequencing](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_f7f7e6466b348191803f2f900098b667).
